'''Herschensohn:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = U.S. Senator | before_election = [[Alan Cranston]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Barbara Boxer]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in California}} The '''1992 United States Senate election in California''' took place on November 3, 1992, at the same time as the [[1992 United States Senate special election in California|special election to the United States Senate in California]]. Incumbent Democrat [[Alan Cranston]] decided to retire. Democrat [[Barbara Boxer]] won the open seat. This election was noted as both of California's senators were elected for the first time. This is not a unique occurrence; it would happen again in [[1994 United States Senate special election in Tennessee|Tennessee in 1994]], [[1996 United States Senate special election in Kansas|Kansas in 1996]], and [[2020–21 United States Senate special election in Georgia|Georgia in 2021]]. Fellow Democrat [[Dianne Feinstein]], California's senior senator, won the special election and was inaugurated in November 1992. == Democratic primary == ===Candidates=== * [[Barbara Boxer]], U.S. representative from [[Greenbrae, California|Greenbrae]] * Charles Greene, perennial candidate *[[Mel Levine]], U.S. representative from [[Santa Monica, California|Santa Monica]] *[[Leo T. Genis (Libertarian) * [[Bruce Herschensohn]], political commentator for [[KABC-TV]] in [[Los Angeles]] and candidate for Senate in 1986 (Republican) * Jerome N. McCready (American Independent) * Genevieve Torres (Peace and Freedom) === Campaign === Initially, Herschensohn was given little chance in the election because of his relatively conservative views, support from the [[Religious right in the United States|religious right]], and the large lead of Democratic nominee [[Bill Clinton]] in the presidential campaign in the state. Herschensohn proposed cutting funding for nearly every federal agency except the [[United States Department of Defense|Department of Defense]], repealing the [[Endangered Species Act of 1973|Endangered Species Act]], banning [[abortion]] with exceptions for rape, incest, and the life of the mothers, replacing the [[Progressive tax|progressive income tax]] with a [[flat tax]], and eliminating federal emergency relief aid for riots and most natural disasters (despite the [[1992 Los Angeles riots|Los Angeles riots]] which had occurred in the spring).{{Cite news |last=Reinhold |first=Robert |date=1992-10-24 |title=THE 1992 CAMPAIGN: Senate Race; Republican Imperils Tide Of Democrats in California |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/10/24/us/1992-campaign-senate-race-republican-imperils-tide-democrats-california.html |access-date=2026-08-11 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Herschensohn also opposed restrictions on international trade and proposed a strong international military presence, citing his views as "constitutionalist." Despite these views, which were generally considered out-of-step with the California electorate, Herschensohn won support with a media-friendly approach, which observers and voters, including women, described as "down to earth" and contrasted with the "overly shrill" Boxer. His years of experience on Los Angeles television had also made him familiar to voters. He also criticized Boxer for her involvement in the [[House banking scandal]], having overdrawn 143 checks on public funds during her time as U.S. representative. In September, pollster [[Mervin Field]] gave Boxer a 22-point lead, but he found that her lead had halved to 11 points by October. No such narrowing was found in the presidential campaign nor the race for California's other Senate seat. Boxer attributed her campaign's issues to early, massive spending by the [[National Republican Senatorial Committee]] to criticize her record. By contrast, Boxer's advertisements avoided direct attacks on her opponent. At the eleventh hour, controversy emerged that the Republican nominee attended a strip club. {{Cite web | url=http://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/sov/1992_general/statement_of_vote_general_1992.pdf | page=14 (24 in PDF) | title = Statement of Vote General Election November 3, 1992 | access-date=December 11, 2008 | last=Eu | first=March Fong | author-link=March Fong Eu | date=December 12, 1992 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080730215019/http://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/sov/1992_general/statement_of_vote_general_1992.pdf | archive-date=July 30, 2008 | url-status=dead }} Four days before [[Election Day (politics)|Election Day]], polls showed Herschensohn had narrowed a double digit deficit, to come within by 3 percentage points. [[Political operative]] [[Bob Mulholland]] disrupted a Herschensohn campaign appearance with a large poster advertising a [[strip club]] shouting "Should the voters of California elect someone who frequently travels the strip joints of Hollywood?" Herschensohn admitted he had visited a strip club once, with his girlfriend and another couple. With [[News media (United States)|press coverage]] of the story, Herschensohn spent the waning days of the campaign denying related allegations.{{Cite news |first=Dean E. |last= Murphy |author2=Shuit, Douglas P. | title = U.S. Senate Candidates Crisscross State for Votes Politics: Herschensohn reacts angrily to accusation that he went to strip joint, frequented adult newsstand. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1992-10-31-mn-718-story.html |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=October 31, 1992 |access-date=March 31, 2010 | quote=A clearly shaken Herschensohn, who has embraced the GOP "family values" platform, at first refused to comment on the accusations, calling them "a pretty desperate thing." But he later conceded that he once visited the Seventh Veil nude-dance club in Hollywood...}} ''The authors were LA Times staff writers''. Although some Republicans later blamed Herschensohn's defeat on Mulholland and accused the Boxer campaign of dirty tricks, evidence of the connection between Mulholland's outburst and the Boxer campaign never surfaced.{{Cite news | first=Arnold | last=Steinberg | author-link=Arnold Steinberg | title=Beware the Trickster: Bob Mulholland oversees the recounting of the ballots in Florida | url=http://www.nationalreview.com/comment/comment111700g.shtml | work=[[National Review]] | date=November 17, 2000 | access-date=December 7, 2008 | quote=That vintage Mulholland maneuver made it all but impossible for Herschensohn to stay on-message during the campaign's crucial closing days. | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090104071050/http://www.nationalreview.com/comment/comment111700g.shtml | archive-date=January 4, 2009 }} {{Cite news |first=John |last=Fund |author-link=John Fund | title = Arnold's 'Harriet Miers Moment' - Has Gov. Schwarzenegger jumped the shark? | url=http://www.opinionjournal.com/diary/?id=110007637 | work=John Fund on the Trail - WSJ.com |publisher=[[The Wall Street Journal]] | date=December 5, 2005 |access-date=December 7, 2008 }} {{Cite news |first=Robert |last=Salladay |author-link=Robert Salladay | title = Governor Faces Revolt in GOP | url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2005-dec-07-me-arnold7-story.html | work=Los Angeles Times | page=A-1 | date=December 7, 2005 |access-date=December 9, 2008 | quote=Bob Mulholland, publicly accused Republican U.S. Senate candidate Bruce Herschensohn of visiting a Sunset Boulevard strip club. Herschensohn had been running as the traditional-values candidate.
Amid the controversy, Herschensohn lost the Senate race to Democrat Barbara Boxer, and the GOP was outraged at what it called a "smear campaign." Kennedy suspended Mulholland, but he soon returned to the party.}} ===Results=== The election was very close. Boxer was declared the winner by the [[Associated Press]] at 1:22 A.M.
